sections.title: What is traceability?

summary.text: Chapter 4 section defining traceability, citing GS1's description as the ability to see the movement of health products across the supply chain, and explaining it as tracing the path of products from manufacturer to individuals, identifying ownership changes and showing products' whereabouts.

sections.extract: The global standards organization GS1 describes traceability as the ability “to see the movement of health products across the supply chain” (25). summary.text: Chapter 4 section on why traceability is important, explaining how visibility of ownership changes helps identify falsified products, protect patient safety and manage product recalls, and noting that traceability systems are mostly based on regulatory requirements, require global harmonization and rely on global standards for interoperability.

narratives.en: Fig 1, 'Public health supply chain partners and processes'. Four nested circles. The outer blue circle holds forecasting and planning and traceability, with the Ministry of health, regulators, procurers, manufacturers/distributors and logistics providers on or near its rim. The orange circle holds sourcing and contract management, procurement and transportation/shipping. The purple circle holds warehouse management, order management and transportation/distribution, with central and regional warehouses on its rim. The innermost green circle holds dispensing, with community health, health facilities and individuals at the centre.

Fig 2, 'Information flow across supply chain processes'. Eight rounded boxes: forecasting and planning, sourcing and contract management, order management, traceability, procurement, warehouse management, transportation and dispensing. Two-headed arrows join them, showing that information flows both ways between the processes; warehouse management is the most connected box.

Fig 3, 'Digital health supply chain'. Six purple hexagons surround an icon labelled Individuals: digital ecosystem, end-to-end visibility, data and analytics, transactional systems, advanced digitization and collaborative processes. A dashed ring around them carries eleven partners as dots: Ministry of health, community health, health facilities, regional warehouses, private sector, central warehouse, regulators, logistics providers, procurers and manufacturers/distributors.

Fig 4, 'The stepwise approach used in this handbook'. Four coloured chevrons in a row: 1. Defining a holistic DHSC strategy; 2. Defining the DHSC architecture; 3. Planning for scalable implementation and sustainable operations; 4. Using the DHSC to implement traceability. Chevron 1 lists four steps (identify and engage stakeholders, analyse the current state of HSCISs, define the vision and strategic goals, define a strategic roadmap and performance indicators). Chevron 2 lists three (assess the current state of HSCISs, define a target architecture, identify implementation activities and map them to strategic goals). Chevron 3 lists four (plan the implementation, develop an operational plan, develop a budget, and implement each intervention). The crop also includes the chapter list and a 'Before using this handbook' box above the figure.

Fig 5, 'DIIG process for planning and implementing a digital health enterprise'. Seven numbered, colour-coded phases — from 01 assessing the current state and enabling environment to 07 implementing, maintaining and scaling — each with its steps. To the right, resource tiles are placed against the phases they serve and marked as PDF or online, including the WHO–ITU eHealth strategy toolkit, the Digital implementation investment guide, the ITU SDG digital investment framework, TOGAF, OpenHIE, the WHO SMART guidelines with digital adaptation kits, and the WHO MAPS toolkit. 'WHO handbook for health supply chain architecture (this document)' is highlighted twice: spanning phases 02 to 04, and in phase 07. Adapted from the 2020 WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide.

Fig 6, 'WHO SMART Guidelines approach'. A top band of five knowledge layers, each fed from a research and evidence base: L1 narrative (enhanced guidelines), L2 operational (digital adaptation kits), L3 machine-readable (machine-readable recommendations), L4 executable (reference software) and L5 dynamic (precision health models). A localisation bar leads down to five matching country adaptations: national policies and procedures, localized requirements, localized machine-readable code and standards, localized digital services, and dynamic applications trained for local outcomes. These feed data, evidence and impact, and an 'Evidence from digital implementations' arrow returns to the research base. Source: adapted from WHO SMART Guidelines.

Fig 7, 'Sample workflow for an antenatal care business, with connections to the supply chain highlighted'. A BPMN diagram with client and health worker lanes: arrival, registration, rapid assessment, danger signs, pregnancy confirmation, quick check, profile and history, the ANC assessment group, the counselling and treatment group (10.1 to 10.9), referral, scheduling and self-care. An enlarged inset shows the tasks outlined in purple as connected to the supply chain: 9 conduct laboratory tests and imaging, 10.5 nutrition supplementation, 10.7 immunizations and 10.9 deworming and malaria counselling and prophylaxis. Source: adapted from the 2021 WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for Antenatal Care.

Fig 8, 'Alignment of national strategies'. Nested arrow shapes, each ending in VISION. The health strategy contains the health supply chain strategy, which contains the medicines and health product strategy. The digital/IT strategy contains the digital health strategy. The digital health supply chain strategy sits where the two families overlap.

Fig 9, 'Inconsistent use of standardized product nomenclature across the supply chain'. A dashed arrow marks the physical flow of health products from manufacturers through the central warehouse, health facilities and community health workers to patients. Below, each holds the same product under a different code: product code 123123 at the manufacturer, A1232 in mSupply, P44545 in eLMIS and AM545 on paper forms, joined by broken chain-link icons.

Fig 10, 'Example of outputs from this chapter'. A table whose rows are the DHSC vision (consistent and timely access to quality medicines through a seamless, technology-enabled supply chain), three strategic goals (system-driven processes, interoperability, traceability of all health products), six strategic objectives with targets such as automating 80% of central warehouse operations, and a four-year strategic roadmap from digitalizing the central warehouse in year 1 to batch traceability in year 4.

Fig 11, 'Health supply chain end-to-end visibility and traceability'. Product flows from manufacturing and shipping through customs, central warehouse receiving and inventory management, distribution, regional warehouse replenishment and health facility dispensing to individuals, with forecasting and planning, supplier and contract management, procurement and order management above. Arcs mark end-to-end visibility at country and global level, and arrows below mark track and trace at national and global level.

Fig 12, 'SCISMM maturity levels for HSCISs'. Five levels of the supply chain information system maturity model, each with its characteristics and an example: level 1 reporting-based (manual, paper or stand-alone tools), level 2 transactional (siloed), level 3 advanced digitalization (integrated), level 4 end-to-end visibility (exchanged) and level 5 digital ecosystem (collaborated). Reproduced by permission from Digital Square.

Fig 13, 'DIIG digital health enterprise architecture framework'. Within the enterprise, a digital health platform holds shared services (business domain and registry services such as terminology, client, facility, product and health worker registries), data sources (institution-based and population-based) and data services (analytics, dashboards, repositories), joined by an interoperability layer of enabling components. Point-of-service applications below are reused across programmes or used for one use case only; external non-health systems sit to the right; a legend marks investment types. Adapted from the 2020 WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide.

Fig 14, 'DHSC architecture framework'. Inside a frame labelled DIGITAL HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN ENTERPRISE: SHARED SERVICES (foundational components: facility, product and supplier registries), DATA SERVICES (analytics — supply chain reports, data warehouse; traceability — track and trace, product verification) and Digital ecosystems (quality, health management information, regulatory, and finance and insurance systems). Below them, an INTEROPERABILITY LAYER of enabling components: authentication, encryption, transformation, orchestration, validation and translation. At the bottom, HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN INFORMATION SYSTEMS (forecasting and planning, order, warehouse and cold chain management, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management and dispensing), beside EXTERNAL SYSTEMS (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories). Callouts explain each layer — for example, that OpenHIM is a useful reference for interoperability components, and SCISMM and TSS v2 for the supply chain systems.

Fig 15, 'Maturity-based architecture: moving from SCISMM Level 3 to Level 4'. The digital health supply chain enterprise has shared services (facility, product and supplier registries) and data services (supply chain reports, data warehouse, track and trace, product verification) above an interoperability layer (authentication, encryption, transformation, orchestration, validation, translation), which connects eight health supply chain information systems: forecasting and planning, order, warehouse and cold chain management, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management and dispensing.

Fig 16, 'Maturity-based architecture: moving from SCISMM Level 4 to Level 5'. The level-4 architecture of Fig 15 with analytics and traceability data services, plus a digital ecosystem (quality, health management information, regulatory and finance systems) and external systems (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories) joined through the interoperability layer.

Fig 17, 'Architecture based on supply chain design: centralized management'. Shared and data services, a digital ecosystem and external systems around an interoperability layer that serves a single set of eight health supply chain information systems managed centrally.

Fig 18, 'Architecture based on supply chain design: decentralized management (option A)'. The same services and interoperability layer, with the health supply chain information systems split in two: at national level forecasting and planning, procurement, supplier and contract, transportation, warehouse and cold chain management; at facility level order management, dispensing, inventory and cold chain management.

Fig 19, 'Architecture based on supply chain design: decentralized management (option B)'. The DHSC architecture — shared services, data services, digital ecosystems, an interoperability layer of enabling components, and external systems — with its health supply chain information systems divided by level. At national level: forecasting and planning, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management, warehouse management and cold chain management. At district level: procurement, order management, inventory management and cold chain management. At facility level: dispensing.

Fig 20, 'Benefits of cross-enterprise analytics services'. Along the bottom runs the physical supply chain: manufacturing, shipping, regulatory customs, central-warehouse receiving and inventory management, distribution, regional-warehouse replenishment, health-facility dispensing, and patients. Above it sit the planning processes: forecasting and planning; supplier and contract management; procurement; and order management. Dashed arrows carry 'Transactional data from systems relevant to the supply chain' up through the INTEROPERABILITY LAYER into DATA SERVICES — analytics: supply chain reports and a data warehouse. A callout lists the questions analytics services answer: optimizing inventory against consumption to minimize stockouts, whether planned supplies will arrive in time, forecast accuracy against actual consumption, on-time and in-full delivery, wastage and leakage, stock at risk of expiry and where to move it, where and how often stockouts occur, and supplier performance.

A small thumbnail of a target health supply chain architecture diagram, shown in the 'Year 3 and 4 – Target architecture maturity to next level' cell of Fig. 21, 'Example of outputs from this chapter', in the Defining the DHSC architecture chapter. The diagram is arranged in labelled boxes: Shared services with foundational components such as Facility Registry and Product Registry; Data services with Analytics (BI reports, Data warehouse) and Traceability (Track and Trace, Product Verification); an Interoperability layer of enabling components such as Authentication, Encryption, Orchestration, Transformation, Translation and Validation; and Health supply chain systems including Forecasting and Planning, Order Management, Warehouse Management, Cost Management, Procurement, Supplier and Contract Management, Transportation Management and Dispensing. To the right, Digital ecosystem and External systems boxes list items such as Quality systems, Health management information systems, Regulatory systems, Finance and insurance systems, Global platform, Manufacturer systems and Data repositories. El diagrama se organiza en recuadros etiquetados: Servicios compartidos (Shared services) con componentes fundacionales como el Registro de establecimientos (Facility Registry) y el Registro de productos (Product Registry); Servicios de datos (Data services) con Analítica (Analytics: informes de BI, almacén de datos) y Trazabilidad (Traceability: seguimiento y rastreo, verificación de productos); una capa de Interoperabilidad (Interoperability layer) de componentes habilitadores como Autenticación, Cifrado, Orquestación, Transformación, Traducción y Validación; y Sistemas de cadena de suministro de salud (Health supply chain systems) que incluyen Previsión y planificación, Gestión de pedidos, Gestión de almacenes, Gestión de costos, Adquisiciones, Gestión de proveedores y contratos, Gestión del transporte y Dispensación. A la derecha, los recuadros Ecosistema digital (Digital ecosystem) y Sistemas externos (External systems) enumeran elementos como sistemas de calidad, sistemas de información de gestión en salud, sistemas regulatorios, sistemas financieros y de seguros, plataforma mundial, sistemas de fabricantes y repositorios de datos. narratives.ar: صورة مصغّرة لمخطط البنية المستهدفة لسلسلة الإمداد الصحي، معروضة في خلية «السنتان 3 و4 – الارتقاء بنضج البنية المستهدفة إلى المستوى التالي» (Year 3 and 4 – Target architecture maturity to next level) من الشكل 21، «مثال على المخرجات من هذا الفصل» (Example of outputs from this chapter)، في فصل تحديد بنية سلسلة الإمداد الصحي الرقمية (DHSC). يتوزع المخطط في مربعات معنونة: الخدمات المشتركة (Shared services) وتضم مكونات تأسيسية مثل سجل المرافق (Facility Registry) وسجل المنتجات (Product Registry)؛ وخدمات البيانات (Data services) وتضم التحليلات (Analytics: تقارير ذكاء الأعمال، مستودع البيانات) وإمكانية التتبع (Traceability: التتبع والتعقب، التحقق من المنتجات)؛ وطبقة التشغيل البيني (Interoperability layer) من المكونات التمكينية مثل المصادقة، والتشفير، والتنسيق، والتحويل، والترجمة، والتحقق من الصلاحية؛ وأنظمة سلسلة الإمداد الصحي (Health supply chain systems) وتشمل التنبؤ والتخطيط، وإدارة الطلبات، وإدارة المستودعات، وإدارة التكاليف، والمشتريات، وإدارة الموردين والعقود، وإدارة النقل، والصرف. وإلى اليمين، تسرد مربعات المنظومة الرقمية (Digital ecosystem) والأنظمة الخارجية (External systems) عناصر مثل أنظمة الجودة، وأنظمة معلومات الإدارة الصحية، والأنظمة التنظيمية، والأنظمة المالية وأنظمة التأمين، والمنصة العالمية، وأنظمة المصنّعين، ومستودعات البيانات. وبهذا الحجم لا تكون التسميات مقروءة إلا جزئياً.
narratives.ru: Небольшая миниатюра схемы целевой архитектуры цепочки поставок в здравоохранении в ячейке «Годы 3 и 4 — переход зрелости целевой архитектуры на следующий уровень» (Year 3 and 4 – Target architecture maturity to next level) рис. 21 «Пример результатов этой главы» (Example of outputs from this chapter) в главе «Определение архитектуры цифровой цепочки поставок в здравоохранении (DHSC)». Схема организована в виде подписанных блоков: «Общие сервисы» (Shared services) с базовыми компонентами, такими как Реестр учреждений (Facility Registry) и Реестр продукции (Product Registry); «Сервисы данных» (Data services) с аналитикой (Analytics: BI-отчеты, хранилище данных) и прослеживаемостью (Traceability: отслеживание и контроль движения, верификация продукции); «Слой интероперабельности» (Interoperability layer) из обеспечивающих компонентов, таких как аутентификация, шифрование, оркестрация, трансформация, трансляция и валидация; и «Системы цепочки поставок в здравоохранении» (Health supply chain systems), включая прогнозирование и планирование, управление заказами, управление складом, управление затратами, закупки, управление поставщиками и контрактами, управление транспортировкой и отпуск продукции. Справа в блоках «Цифровая экосистема» (Digital ecosystem) и «Внешние системы» (External systems) перечислены системы качества, информационные системы управления здравоохранением, регуляторные системы, финансовые и страховые системы, глобальная платформа, системы производителей и репозитории данных. The vision, goals, objectives and roadmap of Fig 10 (greyed), with three new rows: the DHSC target architecture for years 1–2 and years 3–4, an implementation roadmap (enhance the warehouse management system and integrate it with the national product catalogue, barcode scanning, an interoperability mediator, integration of HSCISs, data models and a data warehouse, aggregated analytics), and outcomes such as WMS rolled out to 40% of facilities and the mediator deployed with 30% of integrations done.

Fig 22, 'Building blocks of digital health and DHSC implementation'. Leadership and governance spans the top; below it strategy and investment; services and applications; standards and interoperability; infrastructure; legislation, policy and compliance; and workforce. Adapted from the 2012 WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit.

Fig 23, 'Cost components to determine the total cost of ownership'. A dashed loop labelled 'Total cost of ownership' encloses four groups of cost components. IMPLEMENT: sourcing (RFP, RFI, RFQ), software, hardware and infrastructure, design and development, integration and interoperability, testing and training, and deployment. SCALE: expansion of deployment, training, and hardware and infrastructure. OPERATE: software subscriptions, maintenance (personnel, software, hardware), ongoing training, and monitoring and evaluation. ONGOING: management, governance and overhead. Adapted from the 2020 WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide.

Fig 24, 'Achieving track and trace capabilities through DHSC architecture components'. Along the bottom, the supply chain runs from regulator through central, regional and district warehouses to health facilities and patients. Each location's system — regulator systems, warehouse management, transportation management, inventory management, dispensing, and verification at the patient — exchanges data in both directions with the INTEROPERABILITY LAYER, as do the external systems (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories). Above the layer, DATA SERVICES hold analytics and traceability (track and trace, product verification). A callout lists the questions traceability services answer: where a batch is now, whether supply chain integrity was maintained, who had custody on a date, where a batch was dispensed, whether the product moved through known locations, whether there were anomalies, and whether the product is genuine. A legend defines traceability data as what (product, batch and serial number), when, where and why (the transaction type).

Fig 25, 'Illustrative example of a traceability service interface'. At the top is a mock screen, 'Track and trace results for product 001001123123', batch A1001234. It shows a timeline of five verified events with their location and timestamp: verified and received at the central warehouse (11 Mar 2023); shipped from the central warehouse (5 Apr); verified and received at health facility 001 (6 Apr); verified and dispensed there (10 Apr); and a final patient-side verification of serial number 202 with GPS coordinates (10 Apr, 16:14). Below, the flow that produces it: the manufacturer, central/regional warehouse and health facilities emit ship, receive and dispense events, and handheld verify scans are made along the way. All of these feed DATA SERVICES (analytics and traceability), which answer the screen's query for the product code, batch, its serial numbers 201 to 204 and the expiry date.

Figs 26 and 27, current-state (March 2024) and future-state supply chain systems in Ethiopia. Current state: an OpenHIM interoperability layer, a master health facility registry, a national product catalogue under development and terminology services, DHIS2 and EMR, and supply chain systems including VITAS, FANOS, DAGU, eLMIS, eAPTs and eRIS, with eTrade and eCustom as external systems; a legend colours each by its state. Future state: the layered architecture with an ERP at national level, DAGU, eAPTs and mBrana at facility level, a product directory service, track and trace and product verification, and GFPVAN, manufacturers, eTrade and eCustom as external systems.

Figs 28 and 29, current-state (December 2023) and future-state supply chain systems in Malawi. Current state: OpenHIM, a master health facility registry, national product catalogue and terminology services, DHIS2, QAT and QuanTB for forecasting, OpenLMIS for orders, Navision for warehouse and procurement, eHIN for dispensing, cStock for inventory, GFPVAN outside. Future state: a supplier registry, supply chain reports, a data warehouse, track and trace and product verification are added; E-GP for procurement and contracts, a new transportation system, OpenLMIS and cStock at facility level, and parallel supply chains among external systems.

Fig 30, 'Visualization of future-state architecture from Malawi's SCSA'. Layers from top: analytics and business intelligence (data warehouse, dashboards, reports, traceability, returns and recalls, verification); an OpenHIM interoperability layer; national supply chain information systems (procurement, forecasting and planning, supplier and contract, warehouse and transportation management) beside facility systems (OpenLMIS, cStock, eHIN); a second interoperability layer; and regulatory and foundational components (product item registration, product registry, facility registry, supplier registry, terminology). A global GFPVAN and manufacturers link from the left. Adapted from Malawi's 2022 Supply Chain Systems Architecture.

Figs 31 and 32, current-state (February 2022) and future-state supply chain systems in Rwanda. Current state: OpenHIM, a master health facility registry, national product catalogue and terminology services, DHIS2, QAT for forecasting, eLMIS for orders and inventory, SAGE for warehouse and procurement, EMR for dispensing. Future state: an ERP for supplier and contract, order, warehouse, inventory and procurement management, a new transportation system, QAT, EMR, a supplier registry, supply chain reports, a data warehouse, track and trace and product verification, with GPFVAN, manufacturers and BUFMAR among external systems.

rows: Lack of engagement and participation from identified stakeholders

» Under the leadership of the MOH, establish a steering committee and a TWG and schedule regular meetings. » Identify and enlist a DHSC sponsor (such as a senior MOH leader). » Use the steering committee structure shown in Annex 2.

Relevant stakeholders and/or decision- makers excluded from the TWG or steering committee
